blocks.title: Join and a timer, from scratch
blocks.md:
To run real examples here without a runtime, take the `block_on` from lesson 1 and add two small pieces:

- a **`sleep`** future: it starts a helper thread that waits, then marks the future done and calls the stored waker;
- a **`join2`** combinator, built with `std::future::poll_fn`, that polls both futures on every poll and finishes when both are ready.

They are written out in full below `main`. The interesting part is `main`: two tasks that each "wait", running concurrently on **one** executor thread.

blocks.output:
slow starts
fast starts
fast done after 100 ms
slow done after 300 ms
results 300 and 100; took about 300 ms, not 400: true
blocks.explain: Both tasks start on the first poll, then both are pending. The `fast` timer wakes the executor after 100 ms; `join2` polls both, and only `fast` finishes. After 300 ms `slow` does. The waits overlapped, on one thread. (This `sleep` spends a helper thread per timer for simplicity; real runtimes use one timer wheel for all timers.)

blocks.title: Racing, and timeouts
Tasks and message passing
Do not block the executor
blocks.md: An async task runs until its next `.await`. A long computation or a blocking call (`std::thread::sleep`, `std::fs::read`, a CPU-heavy loop) inside a task **stalls every other task** on that thread. Use the runtime's async I/O and `sleep`, call `yield_now().await` occasionally in long loops, and move heavy work to `spawn_blocking` or a thread.

blocks.title: Tasks or threads?
rows: I/O-bound work: many connections, timers, waiting
an OS thread with its own stack (megabytes reserved)
a state machine of a few hundred bytes

blocks.md: The two combine well. *The Rust Programming Language* ends the chapter by sending from a **thread** into an **async channel**: blocking work runs on a thread, the async side awaits its results. Many real programs do exactly this: async for the network, threads for computation.

blocks.title: join_all from join2
blocks.md: The runtime from the lesson is included at the bottom. Write `join_all`, which runs a vector of futures concurrently and returns their outputs in order. Use `join2` repeatedly, or write it with `poll_fn` over a `Vec<Pin<Box<F>>>` and a `Vec<Option<T>>`. Three 200 ms sleeps should take about 200 ms in total.
hints: Keep one `Option` per future for its output; on each poll, poll only those still `None`.
Return `Poll::Ready` when all outputs are `Some`, taking them out in order.

questions.q: Two futures are awaited one after another: `a.await; b.await;`. Are they concurrent?
options: No: b is not polled until a finishes

questions.q: What happens to the losing future in a race?
options: It keeps running in the background
It is dropped, which cancels it

questions.q: Why must a future passed to `tokio::spawn` usually be `async move` and `Send`?
options: The task may outlive the current scope and run on another worker thread

questions.q: What happens if a task runs a 2-second CPU loop without awaiting?
options: Other tasks on that thread cannot run for 2 seconds
It is moved to another thread

questions.q: Which suits async tasks better than threads?

points: Sequential `.await`s run one after another; `join` polls futures together and waits for all.
`race`/`select` waits for the first and cancels the rest by dropping them; timeouts are built this way.
`spawn` runs a future as an independent task; async channels connect tasks.
Never block inside a task: use async I/O, `yield_now`, or `spawn_blocking`.
Threads for CPU-heavy work, tasks for many waits; programs often combine both.

terms.def: Combining futures so they run concurrently and finish when all have.
Waiting for the first of several futures to finish and dropping the others.
A future handed to the runtime to run independently, like a lightweight thread.
Stopping a future by dropping it; it is never polled again.
Tasks switch only when they yield, at .await points, rather than being interrupted.
